drugs.name: ACE inhibitors and ARBs
drugs.mechanism: Block the renin-angiotensin system, lowering intraglomerular pressure and hyperfiltration, which slows CKD progression
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia and a creatinine rise: recheck creatinine and potassium 2-4 weeks after starting or changing the dose; with ACE blockade, a dry cough for months that can also worsen incontinence
drugs.use: Diabetic CKD once proteinuria appears, and to slow CKD in general; avoid in stage 4-5 CKD and renal artery stenosis; often held the day before iodinated contrast

drugs.name: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin)
drugs.mechanism: Block sodium-glucose cotransport in the proximal tubule, lowering blood glucose and reducing glomerular hyperfiltration
drugs.use: Slow CKD progression (strongest evidence alongside RAS blockade); in CKD with heart failure they help regardless of albuminuria; in type 2 diabetes, fewer cardiovascular events and weight loss

drugs.name: Thiazide diuretics
drugs.mechanism: Block the NaCl cotransporter of the distal convoluted tubule and increase distal calcium reabsorption, so less calcium reaches the urine
drugs.use: Prevent recurrent calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate stones, with a low-sodium (not low-calcium) diet; stopped at least 24 h before iodinated contrast

drugs.name: Potassium citrate
drugs.mechanism: Complexes calcium in the urine, lowering calcium saturation, crystal growth and aggregation; the body's own stone inhibitor is low in renal tubular acidosis, strenuous exercise and high-animal-protein diets
drugs.use: Calcium phosphate stones, alongside a low-sodium diet and a thiazide; recurrent calcium stones with low urinary levels of this inhibitor

drugs.name: Allopurinol
drugs.mechanism: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor: less uric acid is made, so less reaches the urine
drugs.use: Prevents and treats radiolucent stones that form when urine pH is below 5.5, together with fluids and urine alkalinization
